title: 'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight
summary: Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the…

image.caption: Alberta separatists gathered at the Legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29 for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a group whose leadership spurred the Stay Free Alberta citizen initiative petition. (Amanda Erickson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the fight goes on.
Advocates for an Independent Alberta say no ballot outcome will put the matter to rest
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 18, 2026 1:50 PM EDT | Last Updated: 9 minutes ago
"We're never giving up," Jeff Rath, the lawyer for a group that helped organize an independence petition, said Wednesday in an interview.
"The logic of independence is such that we're not going home when this is all over.
"Do you think we're just going to stop advocating for a free and independent Alberta?"
Cory Morgan, an organizer with the Pathway to Independence group campaigning for separation, agreed: "That's a very significant movement on something that's looking for some very serious change."
Morgan said the grievances motivating advocates are still going to be there after the referendum.
"The issue doesn't go away, but it'll change its approach," he said.

items: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests

blocks.text: Even on the pro-Canada side, there is doubt the issue will be put to rest after voting day.

Thomas Lukaszuk, who is steering the Forever Canadian campaign vying to keep Alberta a part of Confederation, said he doesn't put it past Smith to call a second, binding referendum even if a clear majority rejects separation.
"We're making sure that we have the contingency plans put in place to carry on [campaigning] if we have to. I hope we don't. I hope we put this behind us," Lukaszuk said earlier this week.
Voters head to the polls next month to answer 10 referendum questions. Nine of them focus on giving Alberta more elbow room on immigration and constitutional issues.
The final one asks if Alberta should stay in Canada or whether it's time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
The issue has roiled the province. Polls suggest a majority of Albertans want to stay in the country.
Smith has promised to vote to stay in Canada.
She has said she called the vote because of competing citizen-led petitions over whether to remain in Canada or leave.

items: Both sides of Alberta separation debate rally as momentum kicks up ahead of vote

blocks.text: Critics, including the NDP, say Smith has no mandate to roll the dice on Canada's future and that she is only doing so to mollify separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.
Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said a vote for separation is technically not a vote for separation, but a vote to hold another vote.

items: As Alberta separation vote approaches, both campaigns are banking on voter turnout

blocks.text: That means, he said, that regardless of the outcome, Alberta's intolerably subservient status in Canada continues. Central Canada has the majority of the population, he said, and therefore will continue to call the shots in Parliament.
"This vote won't resolve what's broken in Canada and won't fix how Albertans are treated poorly by Ottawa, so demands for fairness will continue," Wilson said.
'Ready to move forward'
Smith has said she expects the Oct. 19 vote to settle the matter.

As recently as this week, her office reiterated that in a statement following a surprising byelection loss by Smith's candidate to the Opposition NDP in what is normally a safe Calgary seat for her UCP.

"In five weeks, the referendum vote will be over, and we're confident Albertans will be ready to move forward and fight for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," spokesperson Sam Blackett said in an emailed statement.
Alberta referendum campaigns heat up
Commentators on both sides of the political spectrum say disillusionment and dismay over Smith calling the referendum played a role in Calgary-Shaw voters punishing her party at the ballot box.
Smith's office disagrees, blaming right-centre vote splitting for the NDP win.
The loss could signal larger challenges down the road for the UCP given Calgary is viewed as critical to victory in the looming October 2027 general election.

Morgan said it's not just voters, but also UCP members that Smith needs to watch out for. He said Smith's embrace of citizen initiative petitions has activated a group of activists who hold significant sway over Smith's party.
"She's going to have to give them something to sink their teeth into or they're going to come after her," he said.
With files from Lisa Johnson
